public_rationale: On January 18, 2026, OpenAI's CFO wrote that the company had about 1.9 GW of compute in 2025. That sentence holds the post's only GW figures, and it never says what is measured: power drawn, IT load, contracted capacity, or capacity actually energized. The figure is called 'available compute' but is not defined, so it does not settle whether the capacity was usable by OpenAI. The claim that the figure was given without saying what it measures holds. The Microsoft and Oracle point was a hedged inference ('would suggest') and is not scored. 'At the end of 2025' loosely describes a statement made in mid-January 2026 about 2025. That does not change the result.
limitations: OpenAI's 'available compute' wording weakens the 'even accessible' part a little, though it gives no definition.
The hedged inference about Microsoft and Oracle infrastructure was not tested.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: OpenAI's end-2025 claim of '1.9GW of compute' would suggest it takes up the vast majority of Microsoft's infrastructure and some of Oracle's, but the claim does not say whether that is active power, IT load, or even capacity accessible to the company.

statement.excerpt: At the end of 2025, OpenAI claimed it had “1.9GW of compute” — which would suggest that it takes up the vast majority of Microsoft’s infrastructure and some of Oracle’s — but it doesn’t distinguish between whether that’s active power, IT load or even accessible to the company.

from_speaker: OpenAI claimed it had "1.9GW of compute"
would suggest that it takes up the vast majority of Microsoft's infrastructure and some of Oracle's
doesn't distinguish between whether that's active power, IT load or even accessible to the company
our_interpretation: The checkable part has two pieces: (1) OpenAI publicly put its compute at about 1.9 GW for 2025, and (2) that statement did not say whether the figure meant active power, IT load, or capacity the company could actually use.
The 'would suggest' clause about Microsoft and Oracle is his own hedged inference. It is not scored.

'At the end of 2025' could mean when OpenAI spoke or the date the figure describes. OpenAI's statement came on 2026-01-18 and describes 2025. The target period covers both (December 2025 to January 2026), so the timing wording alone does not decide the result.
criteria.support_condition: An OpenAI statement gives about 1.9 GW of compute for 2025 and does not define the measure (power drawn, IT load, contracted, or usable).
criteria.contradiction_condition: OpenAI made no such claim, or its statement clearly defined the 1.9 GW as a specific measure, such as IT load or energized capacity available to OpenAI.
